::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.description:
Environmental Exposures and Their Impact on Brain Aging and Health
Environmental exposures can cause acute and long-term impacts on human health (Shetty et al., 2023a). Exposure to concentrations of pollutants such as particulate matter less than 2.5 micrometres (PM2.5), particulate matter less than 10 micrometres (PM10), nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) can affect key cellular processes, leading to unfavourable health outcomes (Shetty et al., 2023b). A lack of exposure to greenspace and a greater exposure to urban factors (e.g., noise and heat) has also been continuously associated with poorer health outcomes (Cacciatore et al., 2025; Kondo et al., 2018). 

The environmental exposome—one’s cumulative environmental exposure over a lifetime—has particular implications for the brain, and can trigger harmful neurobiological effects such as inflammation, oxidative stress, and cellular death (Aggarwal et al., 2022). Furthermore, recent evidence suggests environmental exposures are associated with neurological conditions that arise in older adults such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease (Killin et al., 2016; Ray Dorsey & Bloem, 2024). Older adult populations are especially vulnerable to the harmful effects of environmental exposures due to both the long-term accumulation of negative effects across the life course, and the physiological susceptibility that arises in later life (Risher et al., 2010). Thus, the investigation of the established unfavourable neural outcomes associated with adverse environmental exposures is important for all individuals across the life course, but is especially critical for older adult populations that are most vulnerable to such outcomes. 

The Role of MRI in Evaluating Brain Health in the Context of the Exposome
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a type of neuroimaging that captures various complex and informative measures of the brain, including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM)—all of which reflect different neural properties including brain function, white matter microstructure, and tissue properties, respectively (Hagiwara et al., 2025). The extensive modes in which the brain can be measured allows for detailed analyses of brain changes that can be standardized across aging populations (Hagiwara et al., 2025). Oxidative stress from exposure to environmental toxins can lead to downstream cellular death and brain atrophy, and structural MRI measures of tissue properties can serve as an in vivo proxy for this type of damage (Cannon & Greenamyre, 2011). These neurobiological consequences can also manifest functionally, affecting the connectivity between brain regions (Aggarwal et al., 2022). A measure such as fMRI can be used to measure the correlations between active brain regions, which can in turn give researchers insight into how environmental exposures are associated with outcomes of brain function (Biswal & Uddin, 2025). 
 
Rationale for Systematic Review
The population of older adults (≥ 65 years of age) is expected to reach 1.6 billion by the year 2050—more than double the 761 million in 2021 (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs [UN DESA], 2023). Because of the growth of the older adult population and the unique neurobiological susceptibility of older adults to harmful environmental exposures, it is critical to establish a comprehensive understanding of these associations (Page et al., 2021; Risher et al., 2010). Literature has demonstrated associations with environmental exposures and brain aging (Lin et al., 2024). However, there is a need for a more rigorous synthesis of the relations between exposures and neuroimaging outcomes in cognitively healthy older adult samples. In fact, federal funding agencies such as the National Institutes of Health have published highlighted topics on “Neural Exposome Factors that Affect Brain Health and Neurological Disorders” (Neural Exposome Factors That Affect Brain Health and Neurological Disorders | Grants & Funding, 2025). Therefore, this systematic review is necessary to evaluate the growing number of research studies on these topics to determine trends in outcomes and study methodology, informing future directions of research in this discipline. 

Literature in alignment with inclusion criteria
An emerging collection of literature aligns with our systematic review’s inclusion criteria, with examples including but not limited to:
•	Besser et al. 2021: Associations between neighborhood greenspace and brain imaging measures in non-demented older adults: the Cardiovascular Health Study (doi: 10.1007/s00127-020-02000-w)
•	Casanova et al. 2016: A Voxel-Based Morphometry Study Reveals Local Brain Structural Alterations Associated with Ambient Fine Particles in Older Women (doi: 10.3389/fnhum.2016.00495)
•	Cho et al. 2020: Association between exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and brain cortical thinning: The Environmental Pollution-Induced Neurological EFfects (EPINEF) study (doi: 10.1016/j.scitotenv.2020.140097)
•	Duchesne et al. 2023: Ambient Air Pollution Exposure and Cerebral White Matter Hyperintensities in Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional Analysis in the Three-City Montpellier Study (doi: 10.1289/ehp12231)
•	Qiang et al. 2024: Associations of long-term exposure to low-level PM2.5 and brain disorders in 260,922 middle-aged and older adults (doi: 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2024.142703)
•	Lefèvre-Arbogast et al. 2025: Associations of plasma persistent organic pollutants with brain atrophy, cognitive decline and risk of dementia in older adults (doi:10.1016/j.envint.2025.109756)

We acknowledge that this list is simply the beginning and represents a non-exhaustive effort in delineating impacts and implications of environmental exposures and brain aging, as measured by MRI. Conducting a systematic review will allow us to identify additional papers on this topic and allow such mapping to occur.

Example literature to exclude are those that do not explicitly include cognitively healthy older adults as at least a part of the sample (as confirmed by cognitive testing, medical records, etc…), such as Nußbaum et al. 2020: Associations of Air Pollution and Noise with Local Brain Structure in a Cohort of Older Adults (doi:10.1289/ehp5859), or those that focus on those with cognitive impairment or dementia Power et al. 2018: The Association of Long-Term Exposure to Particulate Matter Air Pollution with Brain MRI Findings: The ARIC Study (doi.org/10.1289/ehp2152).

A preliminary search of PubMed and Web of Science was conducted and no current or underway systematic reviews or scoping reviews on the topic were identified. The objective of this systematic review is to assess the extent of the literature examining the associations between environmental exposures and MRI outcomes in cognitively healthy older adults.

table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants
This review will include studies that enrolled human participants ≥ 65 years of age who are cognitively healthy (i.e., no current signs of cognitive impairment or dementia) to address the topic of healthy aging. The review will focus on human samples who are exposed to one or more environmental exposure, as well as those who underwent MRI brain imaging of some mode. Studies exclusively involving participants without healthy cognition will be excluded to ensure the observed effects correspond to the presence of environmental exposures. 

Concept
The core concept of this review is the relation between adverse environmental exposures experienced by adults aged 65 and over and the neuroimaging outcomes associated with them. This includes both evaluating the exposures analysed and the neuroimaging technique employed. Studies that involve a range or variable number of exposure conditions are included to understand the main environmental exposures and the amounts of exposure that have the largest impact on brain imaging outcomes in healthy older adult populations. 

Context
The context is defined by exposure to adverse environmental exposures including but not limited to PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen oxides, urbanicity, black carbon, carbon monoxide, persistent organic pollutants, heat, and volatile organic compounds. The review will focus on humans who are exposed to one or multiple environmental exposures No cultural or geographic restrictions exist for this review. This ensures the synthesis and representation of clinical and real-world settings. Studies will be excluded if they focus explicitly and exclusively on occupational exposures, such as factory lead poisoning.

Types of sources
This systematic review will consider all study designs, including randomized controlled trials, longitudinal, non-randomized controlled trials, before and after studies, and interrupted time-series studies. In addition, analytical observational studies including prospective and retrospective cohort studies, case-control studies, and analytical cross-sectional studies will be considered for inclusion. This review will also consider descriptive observational study designs including case series and descriptive cross-sectional studies for inclusion.

table.search_validation_procedure: The search strategy was built by the coauthor team with experience and expertise on the given topics explored in this systematic review. The initial search strategy (designed for PubMed) was peer-reviewed by all coauthors before translation for Web of Science. We also used a set of 5 example papers to validate the search.
table.other_search_strategies: Reference lists of included articles and reviews will be checked for relevant papers. In addition, forward citation searching will be used to check for any studies stemming from included articles.
table.procedures_to_contact_authors: We will not be contacting authors.
table.search_expiration_and_repetition: Searches will be updated prior to submitting the manuscript for publication if more than 6 months have passed since the search was conducted in order to identify any newly published studies.
table.search_strategy_justification: As described previously, the author team (with appropriate subject matter and methodology experience), devised, validated, and ran these searches. The coauthor team worked closely with one another to ensure proper keywords and controlled vocabulary terms were utilized. In addition, search strategies were peer reviewed using a modified Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies (PRESS) checklist, and the full reproducible search strategies for each database will be included in the final publication. Two electronic databases were searched - one biomedical (PubMed) and one interdisciplinary citation database (Web of Science Core Collection).
table.screening_stages:
Articles retrieved from the initial search will be imported into Covidence, an online software tool for systematic reviews. Screening and selection will be conducted within Covidence by 2 independent reviewers in the following stages:
1) 2 reviewers will screen article titles and abstracts for eligibility (choose Yes or No). Disagreements between reviewers will be resolved by discussion and if needed, a third reviewer.
2) 2 reviewers will then screen the full-text of selected articles for eligibility (choose Yes or No). Disagreements between reviewers will be resolved by discussion and if needed, a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion will be assigned in Covidence.
table.screened_fields_blinding: The title and abstract will be visible during screening; journal names and authors will be blinded.
table.used_exclusion_criteria:
Exclusion criteria are as follows; papers will be excluded if they meet the following criteria:
- Studies exclusively involving participants without healthy cognition will be excluded to ensure the observed effects correspond to the presence of environmental exposures. 
- Studies will be excluded if they focus explicitly and exclusively on occupational exposures, such as factory lead poisoning.
table.screening_reliability:
Articles will be screened in three phases: a pilot screen to ensure reviewers are consistent in their decisions, and then title/abstract screening followed by full-text screening. During all phases, articles will be screened by two independent reviewers for assessment against the predefined inclusion criteria for the review. Conflicts will be resolved by discussion or by a third reviewer.

The reliability of screening between reviewers will be assessed using inter-rater reliability scores generated by Covidence. Inter-rater reliability (IRR) is a measure of the consistency and agreement between 2 or more reviewers. We will use the Kappa score (Cohen’s Kappa coefficient) provided by Covidence to ensure high inter-rater reliability.

Environmental exposures can cause acute and long-term impacts on human health (Shetty et al., 2023a). Exposure to concentrations of pollutants such as particulate matter less than 2.5 micrometres (PM2.5), particulate matter less than 10 micrometres (PM10), nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) can affect key cellular processes, leading to unfavourable health outcomes (Shetty et al., 2023b). A lack of exposure to greenspace and a greater exposure to urban factors (e.g., noise and heat) has also been continuously associated with poorer health outcomes (Cacciatore et al., 2025; Kondo et al., 2018).

The environmental exposome—one’s cumulative environmental exposure over a lifetime—has particular implications for the brain, and can trigger harmful neurobiological effects such as inflammation, oxidative stress, and cellular death (Aggarwal et al., 2022). Furthermore, recent evidence suggests environmental exposures are associated with neurological conditions that arise in older adults such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease (Killin et al., 2016; Ray Dorsey & Bloem, 2024). Older adult populations are especially vulnerable to the harmful effects of environmental exposures due to both the long-term accumulation of negative effects across the life course, and the physiological susceptibility that arises in later life (Risher et al., 2010). Thus, the investigation of the established unfavourable neural outcomes associated with adverse environmental exposures is important for all individuals across the life course, but is especially critical for older adult populations that are most vulnerable to such outcomes.

The Role of MRI in Evaluating Brain Health in the Context of the Exposome
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a type of neuroimaging that captures various complex and informative measures of the brain, including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM)—all of which reflect different neural properties including brain function, white matter microstructure, and tissue properties, respectively (Hagiwara et al., 2025). The extensive modes in which the brain can be measured allows for detailed analyses of brain changes that can be standardized across aging populations (Hagiwara et al., 2025). Oxidative stress from exposure to environmental toxins can lead to downstream cellular death and brain atrophy, and structural MRI measures of tissue properties can serve as an in vivo proxy for this type of damage (Cannon & Greenamyre, 2011). These neurobiological consequences can also manifest functionally, affecting the connectivity between brain regions (Aggarwal et al., 2022). A measure such as fMRI can be used to measure the correlations between active brain regions, which can in turn give researchers insight into how environmental exposures are associated with outcomes of brain function (Biswal & Uddin, 2025).

Rationale for Systematic Review
The population of older adults (≥ 65 years of age) is expected to reach 1.6 billion by the year 2050—more than double the 761 million in 2021 (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs [UN DESA], 2023). Because of the growth of the older adult population and the unique neurobiological susceptibility of older adults to harmful environmental exposures, it is critical to establish a comprehensive understanding of these associations (Page et al., 2021; Risher et al., 2010). Literature has demonstrated associations with environmental exposures and brain aging (Lin et al., 2024). However, there is a need for a more rigorous synthesis of the relations between exposures and neuroimaging outcomes in cognitively healthy older adult samples. In fact, federal funding agencies such as the National Institutes of Health have published highlighted topics on “Neural Exposome Factors that Affect Brain Health and Neurological Disorders” (Neural Exposome Factors That Affect Brain Health and Neurological Disorders | Grants & Funding, 2025). Therefore, this systematic review is necessary to evaluate the growing number of research studies on these topics to determine trends in outcomes and study methodology, informing future directions of research in this discipline.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in cognitively healthy older adults remains unclear.
Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026.
Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+).
Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought.
The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling.
Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 27 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, adults.
text.formatted: Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 27 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, adults.

text.text: Specifically, we sought to determine which brain structures and functions are most associated with environmental exposures, which exposures exert the greatest apparent impact on imaging outcomes, and how findings vary across study design, exposure window, and methodological quality-thereby mapping the current evidence base and identifying priorities to guide future research and equitable brain health policy for an ageing world.
We developed and registered a protocol for this systematic review with the Open Science Framework (ID# 10.17605/OSF.IO/T453R) and did not make any changes to the published protocol.
We used Covidence software to manage this review (http://www.covidence.org/) and report our review in accordance with PRISMA guidelines.
text.formatted: We used Covidence software to manage this review (<ref type="url" target="http://www.covidence.org/">www.covidence.org/</ref>) and report our review in accordance with PRISMA guidelines.

text.text: Searches were designed, validated, and conducted by the authorship team.
The original search strategy was developed in MEDLINE (PubMed) using the following concepts: neuroimaging, ageing, and environmental exposures.
Once the authorship team reviewed and approved the search strategy, it was translated into search syntax for Web of Science (Core Collection).
We implemented the search strategy on February 23, 2026, and aimed to locate published peer-reviewed studies.

The text words contained in the titles and abstracts of relevant articles, and the index terms used to describe the articles, were used to develop a full search strategy for each database searched (Appendix 2, pages 5-6).
After the full-text review stage, we screened the reference lists of all included studies and relevant reviews for additional eligible studies, which were assessed against our inclusion criteria.
Studies published in any language were included if they had English-language translated versions available.
Following the search, all identified citations were collated and uploaded into Covidence, with duplicates removed.
We screened articles in two phases.
Following a pilot test, titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers for assessment against predefined inclusion criteria.
We resolved conflicts by discussion.
If an article was found to be relevant, it was moved to full-text review and further assessed in detail against inclusion criteria (again by two independent reviewers).
We recorded reasons for exclusion of sources of evidence at full text that did not meet inclusion criteria.
Studies were included if they met three main criteria.

(1) The study target population must include adult participants who were 65 years of age or older and cognitively healthy at the time of the study (i.e., no signs of cognitive impairment or dementia based on screening tools or formal clinical evaluations).

Our registered protocol specified that studies must include adults ≥65 years of age in the sample; as long as this criterion was met, we did not restrict the minimum or maximum age range of the study.
This means that our review retained cohorts whose samples comprised cognitively healthy older adults, but whose age ranges extended into midlife (study mean or median age generally ≥56 years).

Adopting this criterion is important because much of the ageing neuroimaging literature, which were large population and longitudinal cohorts, enrolled participants from midlife onward, and excluding these studies would have omitted valuable data on brain ageing.

(2) The study must include data about one or more physical environmental exposure such as particulate matter (e.g., PM2.5), nitrogen oxides (e.g., NO2, and ozone), greenspace, bluespace, environmental noise, and extreme heat.
(3) Finally, the study must report an MRI brain imaging modality postexposure as the outcome measure.

Studies were excluded if they restricted the study sample to people with cognitive impairment or dementia; focused solely on occupational exposures; or were commentaries and other opinion pieces, editorials, reports, dissertations, conference abstracts, review articles, or grey literature.
One independent reviewer extracted data from each included study, conducting a pilot extraction (i.e., "training" stage) and reliability verification.
A second independent reviewer conducted quality assurance and quality control of 20% of all extracted studies.

We extracted data from each included study that comprised fields such as details of the study sample, environmental exposures measured, their concentration and duration exposed (if any), and neuroimaging outcomes, among other fields.
Data fields collected are noted in Appendix 4 (pages 9-16).
We did not conduct any data conversions or other methods to prepare data for synthesis, including a meta-analysis.

Robust quantitative pooling requires a cluster of independent studies assessing the same exposure against the same outcome using effect estimates convertible to a common metric-conditions this evidence base did not meet.

Although PM2.5 was the most frequently examined exposure (14 studies), the associated neuroimaging outcomes were widely dispersed-spanning medial temporal lobe (MTL), whole brain, white matter, and locus coeruleus volumes, cortical thickness, white matter hyperintensities, and white matter microstructure-such that no single exposure-outcome pairing was reported by more than two studies; the remaining exposures (e.g., PM10, NO2, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, greenspace, and noise) were each examined in only one or two studies.

Effect measures were also not commensurable across studies, having been reported as standardised and unstandardised beta coefficients, odds ratios, absolute volumetric differences (cm 3 and mm 3 ), cortical thickness (µm), voxel-based morphometry cluster sizes, correlation coefficients, and per-interquartile-range increments defined by study-specific interquartile ranges.

text.text: Given this heterogeneity in both exposure-outcome pairings and effect metrics, quantitative synthesis was not feasible, and we instead synthesised findings narratively using an effect-direction approach.
For the effect-direction plot, each study contributed a single representative association.

Because studies did not uniformly designate a primary exposure or outcome, the review team selected for each study the association corresponding to its main exposure of interest and its primary brain structure finding.

Where a study examined multiple exposures or reported outcomes in differing directions, we coded the predominant direction of association across the reported brain structure outcomes and noted mixed findings.
This selection was made during synthesis and applied consistently across studies; all study-level associations are reported in Tables 1 2 3.

text.text: We employed the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklists appropriate to each study design.
Each checklist was composed of design-specific questions that ranged from eight to nine items rated as Yes, No, Unclear, or Not applicable.
Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion.
No studies were excluded solely based on methodological quality.
Methodological quality was assessed using an adapted version of the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, modified by Shan et al,
The quality of each included study was independently assessed by BMW and a second reviewer (KEP or JLM).
The maximum score was seven stars for cross-sectional and nine for longitudinal studies.
Studies scoring 1-3 stars were classified as low quality, 4-6 stars as moderate quality, and 7 stars or more as high quality.
Item-level definitions and the thresholds applied to each domain of the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale are provided in Appendix 6 (pages 20-21).
We report domain-level ratings alongside overall classifications.

We did not perform a formal certainty-of-evidence assessment (e.g., GRADE), because the heterogeneity of exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded the pooled estimates such approaches presuppose; this uncertainty is reflected in our cautious interpretation of study results.
We identified 2,631 records following our initial search.
After removing 135 duplicates, 2,496 records remained and were screened for inclusion.
Following title and abstract screening, 65 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility.
Twenty-five met the inclusion criteria.
Two additional articles were identified from hand searching the reference lists of included studies.
Thus, this review included a total of 27 studies (Figure 1).

text.text: With respect to demographic variables, no study reported outcomes stratified by ethnicity or race.
Two studies reported sex-stratified outcomes while six studies were conducted in all-female cohorts and one study in an all-male cohort.
One study tested sex as an effect modifier though did not report stratified outcomes.

Most studies (19 out of 27) measured participant education or income and subsequently included these as model covariates, not listing them as part of participants' demographic characteristics (with the exception of Thompson et al.); the remaining studies did not indicate education or income as a measured covariate, though three commented qualitatively on sample socioeconomic position as a limitation: Min et al. discussed that their participants had a higher socioeconomic status compared to the general population, Kim et al. reported similar findings in addition to higher mean age compared to the general population, and the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS) papers repeatedly noted that their cohorts were "very white" and educated.
Only Besser et al. treated a socioeconomic measure (neighbourhood income) as a variable of interest.

Six of the included studies drew their participants from the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) and its ancillary WHIMS.
These studies share a common sample of cognitively healthy older women imaged on 1.5T scanners across 14 U.S. sites and consequently are not statistically independent.

The three observational cohort analyses of PM2.5 (Chen 2015, n=1,403; Casanova 2016, n=1,365; Chen 2020, n=1,315, which used data from Chen 2015 to perform an omega-3 analysis) draw on the same first-wave WHIMS-MRI sample, with differences in sample size attributable to analysisspecific inclusion criteria.

The two WHI studies incorporating repeated MRI (Younan 2020, n=998; Wang 2026, n=653) represent the longitudinal subset of women who underwent a second scan and therefore overlap substantially with the baseline samples and with one another.
Petkus 2022 (n=764) also derives from this sample, though its older mean age (81.6 years) suggests a subset that was defined differently compared to other WHIMS-MRI studies.

Because the WHI and WHIMS-MRI studies constitute repeated analyses of a shared population-differing in the exposures examined (PM2.5 and NO2), brain regions assessed, and follow-up intervals-their findings should not be interpreted as independent.

As we could not undertake a quantitative meta-analysis, this dependency was not addressed through statistical means; instead, in our narrative synthesis, we treated the WHIMS-derived studies as a single evidence stream and were careful not to characterise their concordant findings as independent when weighing the consistency and strength of evidence.

Similarly, three studies-Qiang 2024 (n=22,956), Kroeger 2025 (n=36,854), and Thompson 2025 (n=42,802)-were drawn from the UK Biobank imaging cohort and share a common source population; although they examined different exposures (PM2.5, greenspace, and multiple adverse environmental exposures, respectively) in partially overlapping analytic subsamples, they are not statistically independent. Thompson also examined these air pollutants in addition to greenspace and traffic noise.
Exposure assessment methods differed by exposure class.

Most air pollution studies estimated concentrations at the participant's residential address using spatiotemporal or land-use regression models (proximity-based) or government ambient monitoring data; An et al. was distinctive in deploying monitors within participants' homes to capture indoor exposure.

Two chemical-biomarker exposures were quantified through biomonitoring-urinary metabolites (2-naphthol, 1-hydroxypyrene) for polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in Cho (2020) and serum concentrations for persistent organic pollutants (PCBs) in Lefèvre-Arbogast (2025).

Greenspace and related built environment measures were derived from satellite vegetation indices (e.g., normalised difference vegetation index [NDVI] and enhanced vegetation index [EVI]) and land cover or park proximity data from government sources.

Exposure windows, for all potential exposure types, ranged from cross-sectional baseline assessments to as long as 10 years , with 1-, 3-, 4-, 5-, and up to 7-year averaging periods commonly reported; several studies also incorporated a lag between the exposure window and imaging.
Samples of participants with MRI data ranged from 23 to 22,956 (drawn from 260,922 enrolled) and 42,802 (from 85,000+ enrolled), with the three largest samples originating from the UK Biobank.

text.text: T1-weighted structural imaging was used in all studies, primarily to derive volumetric measures.
T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences were also common (used in 11 studies), employed primarily to quantify white matter hyperintensities.
Two studies used diffusion MRI to characterise white matter microstructure-diffusion-weighted imaging and diffusion tensor imaging (fractional anisotropy).
Only one study performed resting-state functional MRI, indexed by the fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations.

Magnet strength was predominantly 3T or 1.5T; the WHIMS analyses used 1.5T scanners across 14 sites, The MRI outcomes included whole-brain volume; grey and white matter volume; white matter hyperintensities; cortical thickness and surface area; hippocampal and MTL volumes (including amygdala, parahippocampal, and entorhinal regions); subcortical and basal ganglia structures (thalamus, putamen, globus pallidus, nucleus accumbens, caudate); ventricular and cerebrospinal fluid volume; and region-specific targets such as the locus coeruleus, anterior cingulate cortex, insula, and medial orbitofrontal cortex.
Additionally, one study assessed covert brain infarcts.

Several studies analysed composite measures related to Alzheimer's disease (AD), such as the AD pattern similarity score in Younan (2020) and AD cortical signature thickness in Crous-Bou (2020) and Lee (2020).
Most studies confirmed cognitive health and the absence of dementia by screening instruments or comprehensive neuropsychological batteries.
Screening tools included the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), the Modified Mini-Mental State examination (3MS/3MSE), the Korean MMSE, and the Clinical Dementia Rating.

More extensive batteries were used by Puckett (e.g., memory, attention, executive function, language, processing speed, and visuospatial ability), Soeterboek (e.g., Verbal Learning Test, Stroop Colour-Word Test, Concept Shifting Test, and Letter-Digit Substitution Test), Lefèvre-Arbogast (e.g., Benton Visual Retention Test, Trail Making Test Part B, and Isaacs' Set Test), Crous-Bou (e.g., semantic fluency, WAIS-IV, and the Memory Binding Test), Cho (e.g., Seoul Neuropsychological Screening Battery), and Lee (e.g., CERAD-K battery).

Beyond neuroimaging and cognitive assessment, additional measures included exposure biomarkers (urinary PAH metabolites in Cho (2020); serum PCBs in Lefèvre-Arbogast (2025), APOE ε4 genotyping, the erythrocyte omega-3 index, depressive symptoms assessed with the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale, and subjective ratings of neighbourhood environment.
Across these cognitively healthy samples, higher exposure to ambient air pollution -most commonly PM2.5 and to a lesser extent NO2 and PM10-was associated with adverse brain structure (Figure 3).

text.text: Reported associations included smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensity burden, cortical thinning, atrophy of the MTL and hippocampus, reduced volumes in AD-vulnerable and subcortical regions, and altered white matter microstructure.
These patterns were broadly concordant across independent cohorts spanning North America, Europe, and East Asia.

Beyond PM2.5, however, findings were not uniformly negative: PM10 was not associated with white matter hyperintensities or cortical thickness, persistent organic pollutants showed no association with medial temporal lobe atrophy, and residential noise was largely null except for white matter and cerebrospinal fluid volume.

Similarly, residential proximity to major roadways demonstrated no clear pattern, with greater distance from a major road counterintuitively associated with higher white matter hyperintensity volume and no consistent association across other measures.

text.text: Regarding risk of bias (Appendix 6, pages 18-19), all 27 studies showed generally low risk of bias, meeting Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal criteria, though ratings were not uniform across domains.

On the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal, most studies met the majority of criteria, but domain specific "No" and "Unclear" ratings were common, particularly for MRI (outcome) assessment and in longitudinal studies for follow-up adequacy.

The five longitudinal studies were of moderate quality in exposure ascertainment and statistical analysis, with risk of bias in outcome assessment and in establishing temporal precedence of the exposure.
The nine observational cohort studies showed consistently low risk of bias, except for variability in MRI outcome assessment.
Similarly, the 13 cross-sectional studies showed low risk of bias, with minor concerns in outcome assessment and participant selection.
Additionally, we assessed methodological quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, adapted for cross-sectional and longitudinal studies (Appendix 7, pages 20-21).
13 studies met high-quality criteria: three of them longitudinal, two of them observational cohort, and eight of them cross-sectional.
The remaining 13 studies met moderate-quality criteria.

Notably, four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criteria for adequacy of cohort follow-up and quality of outcome assessment varied across all three study types, with 12 of the 27 studies not meeting this criterion .
This uniformity in overall judgements may partly reflect the substantial overlap in samples across studies.

This systematic review synthesises emerging observational evidence that greater exposure to adverse physical environmental conditions is associated with differences inf brain structure in cognitively healthy ageing.

The recurrent involvement of the MTL, hippocampus, and white matter-regions vulnerable to AD-related pathology and vascular burden-is consistent with the hypothesis that air pollution (and fine particulate matter, in particular) may act along pathways that increase the risk of pathological aging processes.
Greenspace was more often associated with favourable brain structure though this evidence is weaker and largely cross-sectional.

Finding that these associations were present even among older adults with healthy cognition suggests that environmental exposures may alter the neurobiological processes underlying normal ageing or contribute to subclinical structural brain changes that precede overt cognitive impairment.

In general, the studies synthesised here had limited variability in the types of environmental exposures examined, with the majority focusing on different types of toxic air pollutants followed by access to greenspace.

Exposure to extreme heat was not examined in any of the present studies, even though disrupted thermoregulation can trigger negative effects on cerebrovascular health, and in turn, affect neurocognitive ageing.

Source-specific disaggregation of fine particulate matter may also be informative, as PM2.5 concentrations from wildfire smoke, agriculture, and traffic, for example, have different chemical characteristics that may uniquely impact brain structure and function among older adults.

Previous work has already shown that these sources uniquely contribute to risk of dementia in the U.S. compared to India, but the underlying neural correlates of PM2.5 concentrations in healthy ageing have yet to be assessed beyond the studies synthesised in the current systematic review.

Determining whether the current body of literature generalises to low-and middleincome countries will also be an important future direction as extant studies have overrepresented high-income countries, such as those in North America, Europe, and East Asia.

Not only did participants recruited from these countries have higher socioeconomic status for their respective countries, but there was also a greater representation of female, relative to male, older adults (primarily from the WHIMS cohort).

Beyond this imbalance, evidence suggests environmental exposures may relate to brain ageing differently in females and males-air and water quality more strongly in females, and heat and neighbourhood disadvantage in males -yet because only two of the 27 studies reported sex-stratified outcomes, these differences remain largely unresolved.
Moreover, no included study reported outcomes stratified by race or ethnicity, despite well-documented disparities in dementia burden across racial and ethnic groups.
Replication in more diverse cohorts is desired, ideally with environmental exposures measured over longer windows of time.
No study to date has looked at cumulative effects beyond 10 years.

The most common exposure window was an interval of three years, used in six of the 27 studies, whereas eight studies assessed exposure at a single cross-sectional timepoint and the remaining 12 used windows of one to five years.

Simultaneously, longitudinal assessment of both brain health and exposure will be invaluable for identifying inflection points when the brain becomes most susceptible to certain levels and types of exposure.
Short, recent exposure windows also overlook susceptibility shaped across the entire life course, including sensitive developmental periods.

Prenatal exposure to elevated maternal inflammation, for instance, has been linked to lower hippocampal neurite density decades later in midlife, and exposome frameworks emphasise vulnerable age windows from the prenatal period onward.

With respect to the neuroimaging outcomes examined, all studies but one were limited to structural MRI measures (i.e., regional and total volumes, cortical thickness, white matter hyperintensities) and did not assess relations between environmental exposures and fMRI measures of brain function.

Studying different aspects of brain health in future studies alongside multiple environmental factors in the same sample is important, because recent work (published after the current search period ended) suggests that physical environmental exposures accelerated structural brain ageing whereas social environmental exposures accelerated functional brain ageing.

In general, macroscopic measurements of volumetry and cortical thickness can encompass numerous neurobiological properties, such as decreases in cell density, neuroinflammation, and shrinking of nuclei.

Using MRI techniques that are more sensitive to specific neural processes, such as the microstructure of grey and white matter tissue or brain iron content, are necessary to identify specify biomarkers that can be targeted in future neural or pharmacological intervention work.

The behavioural relevance of environment-related alterations in brain health will benefit from future investigations that directly assess how the alterations help explain age-related cognitive decline, especially those that acquire fMRI measures of brain function while participants perform cognitive tasks.

Here, relations with cognitive outcomes were rarely assessed, and few studies specifically measured memory 12 13,5 7 5 8 5 2 31,32,34,35,37,5 5 28,30,42,45,48,49,53,5 4 5 9 7 5 3 1 3 6 0 6 1 performance and speed of processing-despite these domains showing the most substantial decline among healthy older adults.

Physiological health behaviours (e.g., sleep health, physical activity, sedentary time) and lifestyle (e.g., tobacco usage, alcohol consumption, dietary intake) have also received little attention in the current literature.

Examining these variables is vital as they may help mitigate or exacerbate the negative impacts of adverse environmental exposures on brain health in older adults and act as helpful intervention targets.
Beyond individual risk, these findings may have implications for promoting cognitive resilience and informing public policy.

Because the environmental exposures examined here appear to act at the neurobiological level-producing differences in brain structure detectable on MRI-improving these conditions may strengthen the biological substrate of cognitive resilience rather than simply mitigating downstream risk.

Plausible mechanisms include attenuation of chronic neuroinflammation and related vascular and oxidative pathways, through which reduced air pollution and greater greenspace could help preserve brain regions vulnerable to age-related and neurodegenerative change.

Framed this way, environmental improvement could be one lever at the population level: measures such as lowering ambient pollution and expanding neighbourhood greenspace may complement individual-level strategies and shift emphasis toward community-and policy-level action.

In the longer term, exposome-informed approaches that target upstream determinants such as air quality and social inequality could inform policy, reframing brain health protection as a shared responsibility of individuals and governments.

Because only five of the 27 studies acquired repeated MRI-the remaining 21 assessing brain structure at a single timepoint-this review is limited in the ability to make inferences about temporal sequence and within-person change.

Exposures were unevenly distributed across study designs: evidence for PM2.5 drew substantially on observational and longitudinal cohorts (11 of 15 studies), whereas greenspace was examined almost exclusively in cross-sectional designs (7 of 8 studies).

Two of these greenspace studies reported null associations, and greenspace exposure is strongly correlated with neighbourhood socioeconomic status, so residual confounding by socioeconomic and related factors is a particular concern; thus, greenspace findings should be interpreted with greater caution.

Furthermore, effect measures and outcome definitions were highly heterogeneous, precluding quantitative synthesis; and a substantial share of the supportive evidence derives from shared samples-most notably the six WHIMS analyses and the UK Biobank-based studies-so concordant results should not be interpreted as fully independent replication.

Importantly, however, the PM2.5 brain volume association was also observed in the Framingham Offspring Study, an independent cohort outside the WHIMS and UK Biobank samples, as well as the other smaller independent samples noted in our review.

Because almost all included studies were cross-sectional or measured MRI at a single timepoint, associations should not be interpreted as causal effects, and the cross-sectional volume differences we summarise should not be equated with within-person atrophy or neurodegeneration.

More precise characterization of the underlying tissue alterations will benefit from studies using quantitative MRI approaches, such as diffusion MRI or quantitative susceptibility mapping of brain iron and myelin content.
Residual confounding and exposure misclassification are further important limitations.

The 6 2 2 0 3 2 2 1 3 3 8 6 1 6 3 included studies adjusted for heterogeneous covariate sets: most accounted for age and sex, education or income, and some for smoking, alcohol use, physical activity, APOE ε4 status, or vascular risk factors, but no covariate was adjusted for consistently across all studies (per-study covariate adjustment is summarised in Appendix 9).

This heterogeneity is especially consequential for greenspace and air pollution associations, which are strongly patterned by neighbourhood socioeconomic position and may mutually confound one another.

In addition, exposure was almost always assigned from a single residential address, typically without accounting for residential mobility, time spent away from home, or indoor-outdoor differences in exposure, any of which can bias estimates.
These factors reinforce an association-based, rather than causal, interpretation of the synthesised evidence.

This review points to a consistent, though methodologically constrained, association between air pollution and adverse brain structure, and more provisionally between greenspace and more favourable brain structure, during healthy cognitive ageing.

These conclusions stem from an evidence base that was predominantly cross-sectional or otherwise single timepoint in design, heterogeneous in its outcomes, and drawn from a small number of overlapping cohorts-features that restrict causal inference.
Confirming these relations and clarifying their implications for cognitive decline and dementia risk will require longitudinal, multi-exposure studies in independent, diverse populations.

Combined with such evidence, the findings synthesised here could inform practical, upstream strategies for clinicians and policymakers seeking to protect brain health across an ageing global population by attenuating exposure to adverse environmental conditions.

text.text: (2023) 444 (52.5%) ≥ 65 Montpellier District, France Five years of prior PM2.5, NO2, and black carbon exposure measured prior to MRI using government data (proximity-based) and modelling-based methods One MRI per participant 1.5T GE scanner; FLAIR and T1-and-T2-weighted structural imaging of intracranial volume and WMH PM2.5 exposure was significantly associated with increased risk of being in the third total WMH volume tercile [OR (95% CI) for a 1.7μg/m 3 increase: 1.44 (1.09, 1.89), reference: first tercile] and higher risk of temporal lobe WMH burden (OR = 1.82, 95% CI = [1.41, 2.36)].
NO2 exposure was significantly associated with increased risk of being in the third total WMH volume tercile compared to the second (OR=1.64, 95% CI = [1.10, 2.44]).

Higher exposure to NO2 was also significantly associated with lower risk of being in the second frontal WMH volume tercile compared to the first one (OR for a 14.6-μg/m 3 increase: 0.63, 95% CI = [0.43, 0.93]).
Black carbon exposure was not significantly associated with intracranial volume or WMH.
